Author-reviewed

Cumulative practical · After Volumes 5, 6, 8, 11, 12 and 15

Integrated policy and investment case: the Alder retrofit decision

A project can have fairly priced securities, uncertain social value and a losing constituency at the same time. Recommend a scale of investment only after identifying the effect, reconciling every payment and stating whose agreement makes implementation possible.

Alder is an original fictional economy. Every quantity, contract, behavioral restriction and institutional right below is stipulated for this assessment. None is a market observation, estimated parameter, actual retrofit technology or description of national law. Amounts are in consumption-equivalent currency units (CU); there are dates 0 and 1 and two date-1 economic states, good G and bad B. The unknown causal parameter is separate from these economic states.

Administration and submission

This is one open-resource integrated case, not another closed-book examination. First submit your own calculations, code and decision memo without viewing the reference output or instructor solutions. A suggested allocation is six hours of analysis and writing, followed by a twenty-minute oral defense. These are uncalibrated planning estimates. Preserve the original submission and record assistance, changes and actual conditions. A reviewer evaluates the reasoning and reproducibility, not the resemblance of your prose to the benchmark.

Submit a two-page decision memo; an appendix containing the seven task answers and dated accounts; your executable analysis with documented input provenance; and a short limitations register. The reference implementation and its inputs are provided in the reader package. Reproduce them only after your independent attempt. At least 85/100 and 15/20 in every domain, plus satisfactory oral transfer, is the library’s proposed advancement rule. These thresholds are design choices, not externally validated standards. Invented funding, calling a sensitivity interval a confidence interval, counting a transfer as a resource gain, or concealing a computational discrepancy requires correction and a fresh transfer even when the score is high.

DomainTask allocationPoints
D1 · Mechanism and identificationTask 120
D2 · Securities and valuationTask 220
D3 · Funding and institutional implementationTasks 3 and 6, ten each20
D4 · Distribution and resource welfareTask 420
D5 · Decisions and reproducible judgmentTask 5, fifteen; Task 7, five20

Credit a correct method despite a transparently propagated arithmetic error; do not deduct repeatedly for the same error. A changed recommendation can earn full credit when the original case is solved correctly and its changed assumptions, feasible actions and welfare criterion are explicit. A different unsupported number cannot.

The decision brief

Technology, service and causal uncertainty

The procurement authority chooses a deterministic number of retrofit units n from {0,1,2}. Installation consumes 4n CU at date 0. At date 1, service revenues are 6n in G and 3n in B. Operation consumes n in either state. The developer has limited liability and no other project receipts, so cash available to its securities is (5n,2n). The service-paying household receives gross service value (8n,4n). Service quantity and payment are compulsory conditional on the stipulated procurement contract; this is not a derived competitive demand curve.

There are two households, labeled P and R to distinguish their roles in incidence. These labels do not encode estimated wealth or marginal-utility differences. Each has 10 CU of date-0 cash and 30 CU of date-1 endowment in each state. P alone pays the service bill and receives the service value. Both also receive half of the nonmarket benefit θn−n² in either economic state; a negative value is harm. The n² term is an external congestion cost. Utilities are locally linear in the stated consumption equivalents, and all incremental date-1 equivalents are evaluated using the supplied state prices. There is no additional redistribution weight. This is an explicit social valuation convention, not an inference that an incomplete market prices every nonmarket effect.

The only causal evidence supplied is an exact population treated-minus-comparison difference of 3 CU per unit. Its decomposition is 3=θ+δ, where θ is the effect relevant to this technology and δ is selection bias. A maintained sensitivity restriction is δ∈[0,2]. No sample size, sampling distribution or probability law for δ is supplied. For this exercise the transfer of θ from the comparison to Alder and the additive, state-invariant nonmarket response are assumptions. The observed difference does not establish either assumption.

Claims, timing and funding

Physical probabilities are (1/2,1/2) and the positive stochastic discount factor is (4/5,1). A payoff (xG,xB) is valued at E[mx]. A safe outside productive opportunity is available to bank and developer at the gross return implied by these prices. It converts their unused date-0 cash into date-1 goods without an additional claim on either household or treasury. Its scale is restricted to their unused cash; the economy has no unlimited external borrowing. Household unused current cash is consumed at date 0. Date-1 household consumption is their endowment less the service payment; nonmarket and service benefits are utility equivalents rather than extra cash available to pay debt.

For each unit, the treasury grants 1, the developer contributes equity 1, and a bank supplies the remaining loan 2. The treasury also consumes real administrative resources equal to one tenth of its grant. Equal current levies on P and R fund the grant and this administration exactly. The total appropriation limit is 11/5. The developer initially owns 2 CU and cannot raise additional equity. It accepts procurement when its equity net present value is nonnegative, including zero; the authority, rather than a strict private-profit ranking, chooses n.

The bank initially owns 4 CU of equity-funded cash. It has no deposits, borrowing, capital ratio rule or guaranteed liability. Its total project loan cannot exceed 4. Loan proceeds and contractual face value are different quantities. At date 1 the bank receives min(F,project cash), where F is a single promised face value; residual project cash belongs to developer equity. Select the smallest nonnegative face whose market value equals the loan. The bank and developer invest their unused cash in the safe opportunity. There is no government guarantee and no recourse to either household for a debt shortfall. An installation contractor converts the installation payment into exactly equal real resources, with zero profit; operation similarly consumes its stated resource cost.

Participation and the two decision questions

First solve the allocation problem over financially feasible n without an individual veto, using aggregate incremental welfare W. Compare an explicitly imposed prior that puts probability one half on each causal endpoint, deterministic minimax regret over the whole causal interval, and randomized minimax expected regret. Randomization is over a publicly drawn quantity before installation, independent of the economic state and θ; every realized branch needs its own funding. Nature chooses θ before that lottery, so the criterion is expected regret, not the worst realized regret after the draw.

Then impose a separate institutional rule: each household must receive nonnegative incremental present-value welfare for every admissible θ. These are model rights, not claims about actual law. The authority may enforce a verified date-0 transfer t≥0 from P to R. P pays t plus real transfer administration t/10; R receives t. This cost is additional to grant administration, is paid directly by P, and does not use the treasury’s appropriation. P must have enough date-0 cash after its levy. No outside compensation, future contingent promise or cross-branch subsidy is available. Choose n and a single fixed t before θ is known. Identify which allocation recommendation survives these rights.

Seven tasks · 100 points

  1. Mechanism and identification. Draw or describe the causal chain from procurement to service, bills, financing and nonmarket effects. Derive the sharp identified interval for θ, constructing an observationally equivalent parameter pair at each endpoint. Explain why neither the economic-state probabilities nor the observed difference supplies a prior on θ, and identify two additional empirical checks needed before using the model outside Alder.
  2. Price the actual claims. Derive the two state prices and safe return. For every n, derive the loan face, debt/equity payoffs and their present values. Prove that the stated face is the smallest fair face, including n=0. Calculate expected debt repayment for n=1 and compare it with debt price. Explain default, fair pricing and developer participation without a guarantee.
  3. Reconcile funding by date and state. Show all date-0 sources and uses, including household consumption and safe investment. Check bank, developer, treasury and household constraints for all quantities. For n=1 show both date-1 goods accounts, bank/developer total payoffs and the shortfall from promised debt. Repeat the feasible-action test if the bank’s loan cap falls to 3 with everything else fixed. Distinguish this funding limit from an invented regulatory capital requirement.
  4. Distribution and social value. Derive P’s, R’s, bank’s and developer’s incremental present-value gains. Reconcile their sum with a direct resource calculation that counts installation, operation and administration once. Tabulate both households and W for n=0,1,2 at θ=1 and θ=3. Explain why the grant and service bill cannot simply be added to aggregate social benefits, and what changing social distribution weights would alter.
  5. Choose under ambiguity. Before imposing household vetoes, solve the equal-endpoint-prior problem, the deterministic minimax-regret problem over every θ∈[1,3], and the lottery minimax-expected-regret problem. Prove global optimality rather than comparing only two guessed lotteries. Derive the posterior high-endpoint weight at which n=2 becomes preferable to n=1 and explain what evidence would be needed to interpret that weight probabilistically.
  6. Make the recommendation implementable. Derive the complete interval of fixed transfers making n=1 acceptable to both households for every θ, check current cash and calculate the smallest transfer’s administration and distribution. Test n=2 under the same rule. Identify whether the Task 5 lottery remains available and specify who verifies, funds and authorizes the recommended transfer.
  7. Decision memo and reproduction. Submit the stated artifacts. Report your baseline recommendation, its dependence on rights and evidence, and at least one reason not to implement it in a real setting without further work. Reproduce the reference output after your independent solution, then run the cap-3 stress from a separately saved input. Explain any discrepancies and include an exact or appropriately tolerant comparison method. Do not overwrite your original work or claim that running supplied code independently validates its assumptions.

Instructor guide and complete benchmark

Open only after submitting an independent attempt: seven solutions and scoring

1 · Identification is a restriction on compatible explanations

The authority chooses n, which determines installation, grant, equity and lending at date 0. Installation produces date-1 service; economic state changes both gross service value and the bill. Bills fund operation and security payments. Separately θn−n² changes both households’ nonmarket utility. Selection affects the observed comparison, so an arrow from a selection determinant to treatment and outcomes prevents interpreting 3 as θ without a restriction. Grant funding and compulsory bills distribute effects even if the physical technology is identical.

Solving θ=3−δ gives θ∈[1,3]. For any θ in that interval, δ=3−θ lies in [0,2] and reproduces the same observation; therefore the set is sharp under the stated information. Endpoint pairs (θ,δ)=(1,2) and (3,0) are observationally equivalent. The interval is not a confidence interval, and uniform probability within it is not implied. Economic probabilities concern G and B conditional on the chosen technology; they do not turn uncertainty about selection into a random draw. The half-half endpoint prior in Task 5 is an extra decision assumption.

Two defensible checks are a design-based investigation of selection, using assignment rules and pretreatment information to assess the δ restriction, and a transport/measurement study of whether the comparison’s outcome and population match Alder’s nonmarket benefit. One should also investigate service demand, congestion, delivery cost and the supplied valuation convention. Merely collecting more observations from the same selected comparison may improve precision without narrowing its identification set.

20 points: mechanism with economic/financial channels 6; sharp interval and constructive endpoint compatibility 6; probability/identification distinctions 4; two relevant checks tied to assumptions 4.

2 · Fair financing can contain default

State prices are q=(1/2·4/5,1/2·1)=(2/5,1/2). The price of one sure future CU is b=9/10, hence the safe gross return is 10/9. For n>0, promised face up to 2n is paid surely, worth (9/10)F and at most 9n/5. The loan supplies 2n, so its fair face must exceed 2n. Between 2n and 5n its value is (2/5)F+(1/2)2n. Equating this to 2n gives F=5n/2, within the stipulated region. Debt value is strictly increasing there; lower faces have lower value. Beyond 5n the maximum value is 3n, so no earlier omitted solution exists. At n=0 the loan and all cash are zero; every nonnegative face has zero payoff, and the smallest fair face is zero.

nLoan / faceDebt (G,B)Equity (G,B)Debt PV / equity PV

12 / 5/2(5/2,2)(5/2,0)2 / 1

Equity PV=(2/5)(5n/2)=n, exactly its initial contribution: developer project NPV is zero. The procurement tie convention matters; a requirement of strictly positive developer NPV would reject positive quantities under these terms. Debt’s n=1 physical expected repayment is (5/2+2)/2=9/4, distinct from its price 2. Discounting the physical mean by the safe price would give 81/40, which is also not 2; the debt has state-dependent payoff and SDF covariance. The bad-state shortfall n/2 is borne by the bank relative to the promise. Fair value already prices it. Neither fair value nor zero NPV eliminates risk or creates a taxpayer guarantee.

20 points: state prices and safe return 4; piecewise inversion/minimality with zero case 6; all security payoffs/PVs 4; expectation comparison 3; default and participation interpretation 3.

3 · A funding ledger, not a balance-sheet slogan

Initial resources are 10+10+4+2=26. Each household pays levy 11n/20. Treasury receipts 11n/10 fund grant n and administration n/10. Developer receives n grant, 2n loan and contributes n equity, totaling the 4n installation payment. Bank safe investment is 4−2n; developer safe investment is 2−n. Aggregate initial uses are

4n+n/10+(4−2n)+(2−n)+2(10−11n/20)=26.

This is a resource identity: the loan and grant appear in counterparty ledgers but not as additional real uses. For n=0,1,2 the bank loan is 0,2,4; developer equity 0,1,2; appropriation 0,11/10,11/5; each household levy 0,11/20,11/10. All are within their caps. The largest future service bill is 12≤30. Unused household current cash is 10,189/20,89/10. All procurement quantities are financially feasible at the baseline. Bank net worth is funded by its owner; there is no deposit run or externally imposed ratio to calculate.

At n=1 the bank invests 2 safely and receives total wealth (5/2+20/9,2+20/9)=(85/18,38/9). Developer invests 1 safely and receives (5/2+10/9,10/9)=(65/18,10/9). Their combined safe technology produces 10/3 in each state. Available future goods are household endowment 60 plus 10/3, or 190/3. In G household consumption is (24,30), securities and safe investment deliver total 25/3, and operation consumes 1: 54+25/3+1=190/3. In B consumption is (27,30), bank/developer together receive 16/3, and operation consumes 1: 57+16/3+1=190/3. The debt shortfalls are respectively 0 and 1/2. Gross service value and nonmarket effects are not extra goods or spendable receipts.

With a cap of 3, lending 4 for n=2 is unavailable; n=0 and n=1 remain feasible. An average loan below 3 under a lottery does not authorize a realized loan of 4. Additional equity or outside borrowing would require a changed model and actual counterparties. This cap is a stated cash/loan authorization limit, not a Basel ratio.

10 points: complete initial identity/counterparties 3; all constraint tests 2; both future accounts and shortfall 3; cap stress and interpretation 2.

4 · Private claims and aggregate resources agree

Let E=θn−n² denote the total nonmarket equivalent in either state. P’s net service equivalent is (2n,n), with PV 13n/10. Each household’s nonmarket PV is (9/20)E; each current levy is 11n/20. Thus

VP=3n/4+9θn/20−9n²/20; VR=−11n/20+9θn/20−9n²/20.

Bank total wealth has PV 2n+(4−2n)=4 and therefore incremental NPV zero relative to retaining its initial wealth. Developer total wealth has PV n+(2−n)=2, also incremental NPV zero. Contractor/operation payments exactly consume resources without profit. Consequently W=VP+VR=n/5+9θn/10−9n²/10. A direct resource method gives PV of gross service less operation, namely (2/5)(7n)+(1/2)(3n)=43n/10, plus (9/10)E, less installation 4n and real grant administration n/10. This is exactly W.

The grant is a transfer from levy payers to the developer. The service bill is a transfer from P into operating resources and security payments; charging P and also treating the whole revenue as a net social benefit double counts it. Real installation, operation and administration still matter. Different social weights on P and R would change the objective and whether a transfer cancels in the weighted sum. Those weights would be an added normative choice; they would not change physical cash conservation, security prices or causal identification. The supplied common state-price valuation itself must be defended before a real welfare recommendation.

20 points: household derivations 6; financial NPVs and baseline 4; direct resource reconciliation 4; complete endpoint table 4; transfer/weights interpretation 2.

5 · Different criteria, explicit information

At equal endpoint weights, expected W is 0 for n=0, 11/10 for n=1 and 2/5 for n=2, so choose one. More generally let w be the stipulated probability of θ=3, with 1−w on θ=1. Values are 0, 1/5+9w/5, and −7/5+18w/5. The second positive quantity exceeds the first precisely when −8/5+9w/5>0, or w>8/9; equality is a tie. Quantity zero is strictly dominated by one throughout w∈[0,1]. Calling w a posterior requires an explicit prior and likelihood for evidence relevant to θ; the observed difference and bias bound alone provide neither.

For deterministic regret, compare each quantity with the best quantity at the same θ. One strictly dominates zero for every θ∈[1,3]. The difference W2−W1=9θ/10−5/2 crosses zero at θ=25/9. At θ=1 the optimal value is 1/5, with regrets (1/5,0,8/5). At θ=3 the optimal value is 11/5, with regrets (11/5,1/5,0). For any fixed action its regret is a maximum of finitely many affine functions of θ and thus convex. A convex function on a closed interval cannot exceed the larger endpoint value: for θ=(1−λ)1+λ3, convexity bounds it by the corresponding endpoint average. Hence worst regrets over the entire interval are 11/5,1/5,8/5. The unique deterministic minimax choice is n=1.

A lottery’s value is an affine combination of these welfare functions, so the same endpoint proof applies to expected regret. Any positive weight on n=0 can be shifted to n=1 and increases value at every θ by at least that weight times 1/5; thus a minimizer assigns zero to n=0. Write x for the probability of n=2, with 1−x on n=1. Its endpoint expected regrets are (8/5)x and (1/5)(1−x). The first increases and the second decreases on [0,1]. Their maximum is uniquely minimized at the crossing 8x=1−x, giving x=1/9 and worst expected regret 8/45. This is strictly below 1/5. Every branch still needs the baseline bank cap of 4. The worst realized regret of this lottery is 8/5, so it does not improve the criterion that lets nature condition on the realized draw.

15 points: prior values 3; deterministic endpoint and global argument 4; lottery dominance/crossing/global proof and criterion 5; posterior threshold and evidence interpretation 3.

6 · Compensation changes feasible implementation

For n=1 both household values increase in θ. Their worst values occur at θ=1, so robust participation requires −11/20+t≥0 and 3/4−11t/10≥0. Thus 11/20≤t≤15/22. Cash imposes the additional upper bound (10−11/20)/(11/10)=189/22, which is much looser. The entire stated interval is feasible; endpoint weak inequalities matter. The smallest transfer t=11/20 consumes transfer administration 11/200. P’s worst gain becomes 3/4−121/200=29/200; R’s is zero. At θ=3 their gains are 209/200 and 9/10, total 389/200. The lowest-θ aggregate gain is 29/200, reduced from 1/5 by real administration.

After levy and transfer, P’s current consumption is 10−11/20−121/200=1769/200 and R’s is 10−11/20+11/20=10. Their sum plus transfer administration is 189/10, the same as combined current consumption before the transfer. Therefore the date-0 total remains 26 after adding installation, grant administration and the two safe investments. Transfer administration does not disappear into a financial balance and does not require an extra treasury appropriation under the contract.

For n=2 the worst R gain is −2, so t≥2. P’s worst gain is 3/5, requiring t≤(3/5)/(11/10)=6/11. These cannot both hold. Equivalently total low-θ welfare is already negative and transfer administration cannot make both parties whole. The robust institution permits n=0 with t=0 and n=1 with the interval above. It excludes n=2 and any lottery with a positive n=2 branch because every realized branch must respect these rights. An ex-ante-only consent rule would be different and must be modeled separately.

A feasible implementation appoints the procurement authority to verify n and the treasury to collect equal levies and pay the grant/administration under its cap. P places t+t/10 in verified date-0 settlement, the administrator records the cost and delivers t to R before installation approval. Bank and developer commit their cash before the contractor starts; the bank checks the loan cap and receives only contracted cash at date 1. The committee confirms both household consent inequalities and the authority’s stipulated right to enforce settlement. A real institution would still need independently established legal authority, operational capacity, enforceable agreements and a treatment for failed delivery; those are not supplied by this numerical exercise.

10 points: full interval/cash constraint 3; exact distribution and real cost 2; n=2/lottery exclusion 3; funded verification and authorization sequence 2.

7 · A defensible memo

Illustrative recommendation: “Authorize one unit only under the model’s specified rights and settlement process, with a current transfer of 11/20 from P to R and 11/200 additional real administration. The project then delivers a worst-case aggregate incremental value of 29/200 and makes neither household worse off over θ∈[1,3]. The bank lends 2; developer contributes 1; treasury spends 11/10 including its administration. Contractual bad-state debt loss remains with the bank. Without the veto constraint, one unit also maximizes equal-prior value and minimizes deterministic regret; a lottery marginally improves expected regret but violates branchwise household rights. The cap-3 stress leaves the recommendation feasible while removing the two-unit alternative. This is conditional model advice: investigate identification, transport, nonmarket valuation, enforceability and delivery costs before any real authorization.”

The computational appendix should match every key and rational value in the supplied JSON under the baseline. Parsing JSON and comparing the resulting objects avoids mistaking whitespace or key order for an economic discrepancy. If using floating point, declare the tolerance and compare discrete feasible sets/ties exactly; do not let rounding erase a violated constraint. For the changed cap, the n=2 row is explicitly infeasible with failure bank_funding, and only 0 and 1 enter optimization. Its hypothetical payoff row is not permission to execute it. The reference program reports deterministic optimizers and a prior-weight envelope; the lottery proof is deliberately in the written solution, not falsely presented as a program output.

Record Python version, input change, command, output path and comparison result. The supplied input is synthetic and internally generated, with no external dataset or license inferred. A checksum establishes byte identity, not factual truth. A reproduced benchmark can share the author’s errors; independent primitive calculations and the oral change are separate evidence. A complete limitations register specifies a failure condition and what decision to revisit, rather than listing “uncertainty” without consequences.

5 points: baseline and actual stress reproducible 2; input/version/change provenance 1; conditional memo consistent with the institution 1; concrete external-validity or implementation limit 1. Award these alongside, not instead of, the other six task scores.

Reproducible reader package

Save these five files in one folder. Python 3 with the standard library is sufficient; no account, network, paid service or installation of third-party packages is required. Fractions are stored as integers or rational strings so boundary decisions are exact. Inputs and output use versioned schemas; the code rejects invalid primitive domains and protects source/input/documentation files against output aliases.

  • Synthetic model inputs
  • Reference analysis
  • Exact reference output
  • Run instructions and limitations
  • Four-file byte manifest
python3 integrated-case-analysis.py --output my-baseline.json
python3 integrated-case-analysis.py --input cap3-inputs.json --output cap3-output.json

For the stress, copy the input and change only bank_loan_cap from 4 to 3. Keep your own output separately. By design, running without arguments regenerates the reference output; it never overwrites the input or source. The implementation solves this finite model, not arbitrary policy economies. Infeasible rows can display hypothetical negative cash or payoffs under changed inputs; only rows marked feasible enter its choice rules.

Oral defense and unfamiliar transfer

The examiner chooses one changed case after submission. Allow ten minutes of preparation and ten minutes of explanation, adjusting the time if needed. Grade four dimensions from 0 to 2: correct changed assumptions; valid derivation; funded and institutionally feasible decision; clear limits. Require at least 6/8 and no zero. These scores are separate from the written 100. The examiner must ask why the change matters, not merely request a memorized baseline number.

  1. Information narrows. Replace δ∈[0,2] with δ∈[0,1], justified as a new maintained restriction, not a larger sample. Before compensation derive the new causal interval and high-endpoint posterior switch. Then derive the smallest robust n=1 transfer and its worst aggregate gain. Does n=2 remain impossible to compensate?
  2. A cheaper institution. Set transfer administration to zero, retaining grant administration and all other terms. Find both positive quantities’ robust transfer intervals and the recommended quantity. Explain why abolishing a real cost differs from calling a transfer itself a benefit.
Oral-transfer answer guide

Now θ∈[2,3]. Uncompensated W1 endpoints are 11/10 and 2; W2 endpoints are 2/5 and 11/5. With high-endpoint probability w, W2−W1=−7/10+9w/10, so switch at 7/9. R’s n=1 worst gain is −1/10, giving minimum t=1/10; P’s is 6/5 and the transfer costs it 11/100, leaving 109/100, while R gets zero. The worst aggregate gain is 109/100. For n=2 at θ=2, P gets 3/2 and R −11/10; feasible t is [11/10,15/11], with current cash nonbinding. Thus the old impossibility no longer holds. At the smallest n=2 transfer, worst total is 2/5−11/100=29/100. Under a worst-welfare criterion compensated n=1 is still better. A new prior or decision criterion could favor n=2; do not claim the old posterior threshold automatically applies after unequal transfer costs. Both compensated actions use fixed transfers under the new interval.

For n=1 the interval becomes [11/20,3/4], with cash nonbinding. At its minimum transfer P retains 1/5, R gets zero, and aggregate W remains 1/5 at θ=1. For n=2 the requirements t≥2 and t≤3/5 remain incompatible. Recommend one under the same robust participation rule. Removing administration saves 11/200 at the prior minimum transfer; the transfer itself still cancels from unweighted aggregate welfare. Neither change repairs identification nor authorizes additional bank lending.

Delayed retention and remediation

After at least two weeks without reading the solutions, reconstruct the following on blank paper. Suggested score: two points per item, requiring at least eight of ten and correction of every failed mechanism before advancing. The delay and threshold are instructional choices, not validated retention predictions.

  1. Give two parameter pairs reproducing observed difference 3 and explain what identifies the interval endpoints.
  2. Derive the fair debt face for one unit from its two payoff regions.
  3. Write the direct resource expression for W and identify the two transfers that cancel.
  4. Derive the optimal lottery probability from the two endpoint regret lines and state the timing of nature’s choice.
  5. Derive the compensation lower/upper bounds for one unit and name the extra real cost.
Retention answers

Pairs (1,2) and (3,0) both satisfy θ+δ=3; the maintained closed bound δ∈[0,2] yields the endpoints. One point for compatible pairs and one for restriction versus sampling/probability.

For F≤2 value is 9F/10≤9/5<2. For 2≤F≤5 solve 2F/5+1=2, giving F=5/2. One point for correct regions and one for the fair face.

W=(2/5)(8n−n)+(1/2)(4n−n)+(9/10)(θn−n²)−4n−n/10. Grant and service bill are counterparty transfers; real installation, operation and administration are costs. One point for the expression and one for cancellation.

Equalize 8x/5=(1−x)/5 to get x=1/9 and 8/45. Nature fixes θ before an independent quantity lottery; a worst-realized-outcome criterion gives a different result. One point for crossing and one for timing.

R requires t≥11/20; P requires 11t/10≤3/4, so t≤15/22. Administration t/10 is a real current resource cost additional to grant administration. One point for both bounds and one for cost/timing.

Sources, model boundary and further work

The numerical case, proofs, tasks and benchmark are original. Source roles below are bounded conceptual connections to previously inspected primary material. No source supplies Alder’s data, parameter values or real-world policy recommendation. The causal restriction is solved directly here; it is not an implementation of a published confidence-set procedure.

  • John H. Cochrane, Asset Pricing, author-hosted sample chapters: the previously inspected 2001-copyright copy’s printed pages 6–11 and 17–20 support the SDF/payoff distinction and covariance pricing context. This case supplies its own finite prices and no empirical calibration.
  • Farag, Harland and Nixon, “Bank capital and liquidity,” Bank of England (2013): previously inspected pages 201–207 and 209 provide historical conceptual context for balance sheets, funding and liquidity. No then-current regulatory threshold or accounting rule is imported.
  • Rambachan and Roth, “A More Credible Approach to Parallel Trends”: previously inspected physical pages 1–12 motivate explicitly restricted departures and sensitivity. Alder’s exact population identity is not their estimator or inference procedure; no finite-sample coverage is claimed.
  • Besley and Persson, “The Origins of State Capacity,” author-hosted manuscript: previously inspected physical pages 1–5 motivate treating administrative capability and timing as substantive assumptions. Alder’s costs and authority are stipulated, not estimated from that paper.

The case connects accepted methods; it cannot establish empirical identification, legal enforceability, a universal social valuation rule or learner professional competence. A useful next research step is to identify which assumption can realistically be investigated and how the resulting evidence would alter the decision. The research volume develops that transition from a solved teaching model to a defensible original question.
